title: Gravitation

toc.title: 6.1 Newton's law of gravitation; acceleration due to gravity and its variation
6.2 Gravitational field strength, potential and potential energy
6.3 Satellites: orbital velocity, period, energy, escape velocity, geostationary orbit

html:
Gravitation is the one force that never switches off: it holds the Moon in its orbit, keeps your feet on the ground in Kathmandu and makes a dropped stone fall the same way everywhere on Earth. Of the 10 Mechanics questions in the Physics paper (official weightage), we estimate about 1 comes from this chapter. It is almost always a comparison rather than a calculation: g at a height against g at a depth, escape speed against orbital speed, or a "which statement is true" about the energy of a satellite. Learn the two variation formulas and the sign of the energy, and the mark is quick.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • F = Gm_1m_2/r^2 and g = GM/R^2; G = 6.67\times10^{-11} N m² kg⁻².
  • Height: g_h = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2; depth: g_d = g\left(1-\frac{d}{R}\right) — linear, not inverse-square.
  • Latitude: g_\lambda = g - R\omega^2\cos^2\lambda; least at the equator, greatest at the poles.
  • Field strength GM/r^2 (N kg⁻¹); potential -GM/r (J kg⁻¹); potential energy -GMm/r.
  • Orbital speed v = \sqrt{GM/r}; period T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}, so T^2 \propto r^3.
  • Satellite energy: K = GMm/2r, U = -GMm/r, E = -GMm/2r — the total is negative.
  • Escape speed v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{2gR} = 11.2 km s⁻¹, and v_e = \sqrt{2}\,v_{orbital}.
  • Geostationary orbit: period 24 h, above the equator, west to east, height about 36,000 km.

6.1 Newton's law of gravitation; acceleration due to gravity and its variation

The inverse-square law

Newton's law of gravitation

Every particle of matter attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The force acts along the line joining the particles.

F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}

Here m_1 and m_2 are the masses, r the distance between their centres, and G the universal gravitational constant:

G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\text{kg}^{-2}

In vector form, the force on m_1 due to m_2 is \vec F_{12} = -\frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\hat r, where \hat r points from m_1 to m_2; the minus sign is what makes the force attractive.

Property Meaning
Universal The same value of G everywhere, for every pair of masses
Always attractive There is no gravitational repulsion
Mutual The two forces are an action–reaction pair, equal and opposite, on different bodies
Central Acts along the line joining the centres
Conservative Work done depends only on the end points, so a potential energy exists
Independent of the medium No medium is needed; it is not weakened by a vacuum
Long range, weakest Infinite range, but about 10^{36} times weaker than the electrostatic force between two protons

The law was stated for point masses. It also holds, exactly, for two uniform spheres with r measured between their centres — a result Newton proved with the shell theorem. That is why we may treat the whole Earth as a point at its centre.

g at the surface of a planet

For a body of mass m on the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R, the gravitational force is its weight:

mg = \frac{GMm}{R^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g = \frac{GM}{R^2}

So g is fixed by the planet, not by the falling body: a feather and a hammer have the same g (they fall differently only because of air resistance). With M = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3\rho,

g = \frac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R

Two planets of the same density have surface gravities proportional to their radii.

Body g (m s⁻²)
Earth (mean) 9.8
Moon 1.62
Mars 3.7
Jupiter 24.8
Sun 274

On the Moon g is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so a 60 kg astronaut weighs about 590 N on Earth but only 97 N on the Moon — the mass is 60 kg in both places.

Variation with altitude

At a height h above the surface the distance from the centre is R+h, so

g_h = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2

For h \ll R we may expand:

g_h \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)

so a small height lowers g by the fraction 2h/R. The exact formula must be used when h is comparable with R.

Height g_h
h = R g/4
h = 2R g/9
h = 3R g/16
h \to \infty 0

Variation with depth — and the mistake almost everyone makes

At a depth d below the surface the body is at distance R-d from the centre. The temptation is to write g_d = GM/(R-d)^2, which would make g increase with depth. That is wrong: the matter outside radius R-d does not pull on the body at all, so the mass that matters is smaller too.

Shell theorem. A uniform spherical shell exerts no net gravitational force on a particle anywhere inside it. So at depth d only the sphere of radius R-d matters; the shell of thickness d outside that radius pulls equally in all directions and cancels.

Assuming the Earth has uniform density \rho,

M' = \frac{4}{3}\pi (R-d)^3\rho = M\frac{(R-d)^3}{R^3}

g_d = \frac{GM'}{(R-d)^2} = \frac{GM(R-d)}{R^3} = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)

The variation with depth is linear: g falls steadily from g at the surface to zero at the centre.

Depth g_d
d = R/4 3g/4
d = R/2 g/2
d = 3R/4 g/4
d = R 0

The depth formula is linear — and it is not the height formula

At a height h the whole Earth still pulls, so g falls as (R/(R+h))^2. At a depth d the outer shell stops pulling, so g falls as (R-d)/R. A 1 % drop needs d = 0.01R \approx 64 km but only h \approx 0.005R \approx 32 km. Any option that uses (R-d)^2 in the denominator is a distractor built on exactly this error.

The formula assumes uniform density

The real Earth is denser at the core, so g actually stays close to 9.8 and even rises slightly down to the core–mantle boundary before falling to zero. The linear law g_d = g(1-d/R) is the one the syllabus and the paper use, and it is exact only for a uniform sphere.

Variation with latitude and the shape of the Earth

A body at latitude \lambda is not at rest in an inertial frame: it goes round the Earth's axis once a day in a circle of radius R\cos\lambda, with angular speed \omega = 2\pi/(24\times3600) = 7.27\times10^{-5} rad s⁻¹. Part of gravity must supply this centripetal acceleration, which points towards the axis. Resolving along the local vertical gives the effective value:

g_\lambda = g - R\omega^2\cos^2\lambda

  • At the poles (\lambda = 90^{\circ}): \cos\lambda = 0, so g is unchanged — maximum.
  • At the equator (\lambda = 0^{\circ}): the reduction is greatest, R\omega^2 \approx 0.034 m s⁻².

The Earth is also slightly oblate — the equatorial radius (6378 km) is larger than the polar radius (6357 km) — which lowers g at the equator further. The two effects together give about 9.78 m s⁻² at the equator and 9.83 m s⁻² at the poles. A body taken from the equator to a pole therefore loses a little weight but keeps its mass.

Worked example 6.1 — height against depth

Problem. Taking R = 6400 km, at what depth and at what height is g less than its surface value by 1 %?

Solution. Depth: g_d = g(1-d/R), so d/R = 0.01 and d = 0.01\times6400 = 64 km.

Height: g_h = g(R/(R+h))^2. For a 1 % drop, R/(R+h) = \sqrt{0.99} = 0.995, so h = 6400(1/0.995 - 1) = 32.2 km. The approximation 2h/R = 0.01 gives the same 32 km.

The height needed is half the depth: near the surface the inverse-square fall is twice as fast as the linear one.

Worked example 6.2 — the equator–pole weight difference

Problem. A student of mass 70 kg is weighed at the equator and at a pole. Taking R = 6.4\times10^6 m and the rotation period as 24 h, find the difference in weight caused by the Earth's rotation alone.

Solution. \omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi/86400 = 7.27\times10^{-5} rad s⁻¹.

At the equator the reduction is R\omega^2 = (6.4\times10^6)(7.27\times10^{-5})^2 = 0.034 m s⁻².

So \Delta W = m\Delta g = 70\times0.034 = 2.4 N. The weight at the pole is about 686 N, so rotation changes it by only 0.35 % — a real effect, but a small one. The rest of the pole–equator difference comes from the Earth's flattening.

Three formulas, three behaviours

Height: square in the denominator — falls fast, g/4 at h = R. Depth: linear — falls slowly, zero at the centre. Latitude: cosine squared — no effect at the poles, largest at the equator.

6.2 Gravitational field strength, potential and potential energy

Field strength

The gravitational field strength at a point is the gravitational force per unit mass placed there:

\vec E_g = \frac{\vec F}{m} = -\frac{GM}{r^2}\hat r

Its magnitude is GM/r^2 and its SI unit is N kg⁻¹, which is identical to m s⁻² — the field strength is the local acceleration of free fall. Near the Earth's surface it is 9.8 N kg⁻¹ downwards.

Field lines point towards the mass, radially. Their density shows the strength: close to the Earth the lines are crowded, far away they are spread out. Field lines never cross (a point cannot have two directions of force), and they are perpendicular to the equipotential surfaces.

Field is a vector; potential is a scalar

"Do not confuse GM/r^2 with GM/r." The field is force per unit mass (N kg⁻¹) and falls as 1/r^2; the potential is energy per unit mass (J kg⁻¹) and falls as 1/r. At the surface, E_g = g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ while V = -gR = -6.3\times10^7 J kg⁻¹.

Potential

Gravitational potential

The gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass by an external agent in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point, without acceleration.

V = -\frac{GM}{r}

The zero is chosen at infinity. Because gravity attracts, the agent does negative work as the mass comes in from infinity, so V is negative everywhere at a finite distance and rises towards zero at infinity.

Quantity Expression Unit Sign
Field strength GM/r^2 N kg⁻¹ magnitude, direction towards M
Potential -GM/r J kg⁻¹ always negative
Potential energy of m -GMm/r J always negative

The field is the negative gradient of the potential:

E_g = -\frac{dV}{dr}

so on a graph of V against r the field is minus the slope. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work, because the displacement is perpendicular to the force.

Potential energy

U = -\frac{GMm}{r}

The change in potential energy when a mass moves from r_1 to r_2 is

\Delta U = GMm\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right)

Moving away from the Earth (r_2 > r_1) makes \Delta U positive: the external agent must do work. Moving towards the Earth makes it negative: gravity does the work.

For a small height h above the surface, put r_1 = R and r_2 = R+h:

\Delta U = \frac{GMmh}{R(R+h)} \approx \frac{GMmh}{R^2} = mgh

So the familiar mgh is only the near-surface approximation of -GMm/r. It fails when h is a large fraction of R.

Sign conventions that decide the answer
  • U = 0 at infinity, and U is negative at every finite distance.
  • A bound body (a satellite, the Moon) has negative total energy.
  • "Increases" always means becomes less negative when a body moves outward.
  • The work done by gravity is -\Delta U; the work done by an external agent is +\Delta U. The paper often asks for one and offers the other.

Field and potential inside a sphere

Region Field Potential
Inside a thin shell 0 constant, -GM/R (same as the surface)
Inside a uniform solid sphere, radius r GMr/R^3 -\frac{GM}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)
At the centre of a solid sphere 0 -3GM/2R (minimum)

Inside a shell the field is zero but the potential is not zero: no force is needed to move about inside, yet work was needed to bring the mass from infinity to the shell. This distinction is a favourite "which statement is true" question.

Distance from the centre E_g (N kg⁻¹) V (J kg⁻¹)
R (surface) 9.8 -6.3\times10^7
2R 2.45 -3.1\times10^7
3R 1.09 -2.1\times10^7
\infty 0 0

Doubling the distance quarters the field but only halves the magnitude of the potential — the 1/r^2 against 1/r difference again.

Worked example 6.3 — potential, field and the work to climb

Problem. A body of mass 5 kg is on the Earth's surface (R = 6400 km, g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find (i) the potential and field at a distance 2R from the centre, and (ii) the work needed to take the body from the surface to that point.

Solution. With GM = gR^2:

(i) V = -GM/(2R) = -gR/2 = -(9.8)(6.4\times10^6)/2 = -3.1\times10^7 J kg⁻¹. E_g = GM/(2R)^2 = g/4 = 2.45 N kg⁻¹, towards the Earth.

(ii) U_1 = -GMm/R = -mgR = -(5)(9.8)(6.4\times10^6) = -3.14\times10^8 J. U_2 = -GMm/2R = -1.57\times10^8 J. Work by the agent = U_2 - U_1 = 1.57\times10^8 J.

Note that mgh would give 5\times9.8\times6.4\times10^6 = 3.14\times10^8 J — twice the true answer, because h = R is not small.

6.3 Satellites: orbital velocity, period, energy, escape velocity, geostationary orbit

A satellite stays in a circular orbit because gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force it needs. There is no "centrifugal force" pushing it out; the single force is the pull of the Earth, directed to the centre.

Orbital velocity

For a satellite of mass m in a circular orbit of radius r (measured from the Earth's centre) at speed v:

\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}

The mass of the satellite cancels: a 1 kg CubeSat and a 400-tonne space station at the same radius move at the same speed. Near the surface (r \approx R),

v_{orb} = \sqrt{gR} = \sqrt{(9.8)(6.4\times10^6)} = 7.9\ \text{km s}^{-1}

Higher orbits are slower: v \propto 1/\sqrt{r}.

Newton's cannonball. Fire a ball horizontally from a very high mountain. It lands a short way off; fired faster, it lands farther; at 7.9 km s⁻¹ the ground curves away as quickly as the ball falls and it never lands. An orbit is not a place where gravity is absent — it is a fall that never reaches the ground.

Period

The satellite covers 2\pi r in one period T, so v = 2\pi r/T:

T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}

Squaring, T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3, so

T^2 \propto r^3

which is Kepler's third law. For a satellite skimming the surface, T = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g} = 84.6 min — the lowest possible orbital period around the Earth.

Orbit Radius Period
Surface-skimming R 84.6 min
400 km (ISS) 1.06R about 1.5 h
GPS 26\,600 km about 12 h
Geostationary 42\,200 km 24 h
Moon 3.84\times10^8 m 27.3 days

Energy of a satellite

K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{GMm}{2r}, \qquad U = -\frac{GMm}{r}

E = K + U = -\frac{GMm}{2r}

Three relations follow at once, and the paper uses all three:

E = -K, \qquad U = 2E, \qquad U = -2K

  • The total energy is negative: the satellite is bound.
  • The binding energy — the energy needed to remove it to infinity — is +GMm/2r.
  • As r increases, K and the magnitude of U both decrease, but E becomes less negative, that is, it increases. Moving a satellite to a higher orbit costs energy even though it ends up moving more slowly.
"Higher orbit" means slower but more energetic

Students remember "higher is slower" and then conclude "higher has less energy". Both statements are true but about different quantities: K decreases, E increases. To lift a satellite from r_1 to r_2 the rocket must supply \frac{GMm}{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_1}-\frac{1}{r_2}\right).

Escape velocity

The escape velocity is the minimum speed at the surface needed to just reach infinity. At infinity both K and U are zero, so the total energy at launch must be at least zero:

\frac{1}{2}mv_e^2 - \frac{GMm}{R} = 0

v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}

For the Earth, v_e = \sqrt{2(9.8)(6.4\times10^6)} = 1.12\times10^4 m s⁻¹ = 11.2 km s⁻¹.

Feature Orbital speed Escape speed
Formula \sqrt{GM/r} \sqrt{2GM/R}
Earth value 7.9 km s⁻¹ 11.2 km s⁻¹
Depends on radius of the orbit mass and radius of the planet
Depends on satellite mass no no
Direction along the orbit any direction (ignoring air and rotation)

Since v_e = \sqrt{2}\,\sqrt{GM/R} = \sqrt{2}\,v_{orb} at the surface, the escape speed is 1.414 times the orbital speed. That ratio \sqrt{2} is one of the most reliable one-mark questions in the chapter.

Escape speed does not depend on the mass of the escaping body, and (in the idealised problem) not on the direction of projection — a stone thrown horizontally at 11.2 km s⁻¹ escapes just as a vertical one does, though the ground gets in the way.

Geostationary orbit

A geostationary satellite stays above the same point of the Earth. For that it must satisfy three conditions:

  1. Period 24 h — actually one sidereal day, 23 h 56 min 4 s, the time for one rotation relative to the stars.
  2. Above the equator — an orbit over any other latitude would drift north and south.
  3. West to east, the same sense as the Earth's rotation.

Putting T = 86400 s into r = (GMT^2/4\pi^2)^{1/3} gives r = 4.22\times10^7 m, so the height above the surface is

h = 4.22\times10^7 - 6.4\times10^6 \approx 3.6\times10^7\ \text{m} = 36\,000\ \text{km}

There is only one geostationary radius, so all such satellites share a single ring — the geostationary belt. Their orbital speed is about 3.1 km s⁻¹. They are used for television, telephone and weather satellites, because a dish on the ground can be fixed pointing at one spot.

Geostationary Polar (sun-synchronous)
Orbit equatorial, circular passes over the poles
Period 24 h about 90–100 min
Height 36,000 km 600–1000 km
Ground track fixed point whole Earth as it turns
Used for communication, weather remote sensing, mapping, spy satellites

Why launches go east, and from low latitudes

A point on the equator is already moving east at R\omega = 465 m s⁻¹ because of the Earth's rotation (check: 6.4\times10^6 \times 7.27\times10^{-5}). A rocket launched eastward from near the equator starts with that speed for free, so it needs less fuel to reach 7.9 km s⁻¹. A launch from a higher latitude gets less help (the speed is 465\cos\lambda m s⁻¹), and a polar launch gets none at all. This is why space agencies build launch sites as close to the equator as they can, and why almost all communication satellites are launched eastward.

Weightlessness in orbit

An astronaut in the International Space Station is not outside gravity: at 400 km, g = 9.8(6400/6800)^2 = 8.7 m s⁻², only 11 % less than on the ground. The station and the astronaut are both falling freely with the same acceleration, so the floor never pushes on them. The normal reaction is zero, and that is what "weightlessness" means. The same thing happens for a few seconds in a lift whose cable snaps.

Worked example 6.4 — a satellite at height 2R

Problem. A satellite orbits at a height 2R above the Earth's surface (R = 6400 km, g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find its orbital speed and period.

Solution. Here r = 3R, so v = \sqrt{GM/3R} = \sqrt{gR/3} = 7.9/\sqrt{3} = 4.6 km s⁻¹.

T = 2\pi\sqrt{(3R)^3/GM} = 2\pi\sqrt{27R/g} = 84.6\sqrt{27} min = 84.6\times5.20 = 440 min \approx 7.3 h.

Check with Kepler: the surface-skimming period is 84.6 min at r = R; at r = 3R the period is 3^{3/2} = 5.2 times larger.

Worked example 6.5 — escape speed of another planet

Problem. A planet has twice the mass and half the radius of the Earth. Find its escape speed in terms of the Earth's 11.2 km s⁻¹.

Solution. v_e \propto \sqrt{M/R}, so

\frac{v_e'}{v_e} = \sqrt{\frac{2M}{M}\cdot\frac{R}{R/2}} = \sqrt{4} = 2

The escape speed is 2\times11.2 = 22.4 km s⁻¹. A smaller radius more than makes up for the larger mass, because the body starts deeper in the potential well.

Formula and fact sheet

Field strength E_g = GM/r^2, N kg⁻¹; E_g = -dV/dr

Inside a shell E_g = 0, V = -GM/R (constant)
Inside a solid sphere E_g = GMr/R^3; V = -\frac{GM}{2R^3}(3R^2-r^2)

Chapter summary

  • Every mass attracts every other with F = Gm_1m_2/r^2; the force is always attractive, mutual, central and conservative.
  • Surface gravity is g = GM/R^2; it belongs to the planet, not to the falling body.
  • With height g_h = g(R/(R+h))^2 (inverse square); with depth g_d = g(1-d/R) (linear, because the outer shell pulls equally all round). g is zero at the centre.
  • Rotation reduces g most at the equator: g_\lambda = g - R\omega^2\cos^2\lambda; the poles have the largest g and the equator the smallest.
  • Field strength GM/r^2 is a vector in N kg⁻¹; potential -GM/r is a scalar in J kg⁻¹, zero at infinity and negative everywhere else.
  • Potential energy is -GMm/r; mgh is only its near-surface approximation. The work by an external agent is +\Delta U.
  • Orbital speed \sqrt{GM/r} and period 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}: higher orbits are slower, and T^2 \propto r^3.
  • Satellite energy: K = GMm/2r, U = -GMm/r, E = -GMm/2r. The total is negative and equals -K; raising the orbit increases E but decreases K.
  • Escape speed \sqrt{2GM/R} = 11.2 km s⁻¹ is \sqrt{2} times the surface orbital speed and is independent of the body's mass.
  • A geostationary satellite needs 24 h, the equatorial plane and west-to-east motion; its height is about 36,000 km.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (a) — potential is work per unit mass, J kg⁻¹. N kg⁻¹ is field strength, and N m² kg⁻² is G.

2. (d) — G = 6.67\times10^{-11} N m² kg⁻². The value 9.8 is g (a local acceleration), and option (b) carries the wrong units for G.

3. (c) — at the centre the mass inside the body's radius is zero, so by the shell theorem the pull is zero.

4. (d) — only the sphere of radius R-d pulls, giving g(R-d)/R = g(1-d/R). Option (b) is the common error of applying the height formula downwards.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (a) — the depth formula is g(1-d/R); at d = R it gives zero. The height case keeps the whole Earth pulling, so it only falls to g/4.

2. (d) — v = \sqrt{GM/r} has no mass in it, so the speeds are equal; K = GMm/2r is proportional to the satellite's mass, so the kinetic energies differ.

3. (b) — E = -GMm/2r is negative for every bound orbit. K is positive and U is negative, so (a) and (c) are impossible.

4. (d) — v \propto 1/\sqrt{r} falls, while E = -GMm/2r becomes less negative, that is, it rises.

5. (d) — g at 400 km is still 8.7 m s⁻²; the astronaut floats because both craft and astronaut are in free fall, so the normal reaction vanishes.

9. (b) — V = -3GM/2R at the centre, more negative than the surface value -GM/R; the potential is least (most negative) there.

10. (c) — v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R}; the Moon's M is 1/81 and R about 1/3.7 of the Earth's, so v_e falls to 2.4 km s⁻¹. The absence of an atmosphere is a consequence, not the cause.

11. (d) — T \propto r^{3/2}, so doubling r multiplies T by 2^{3/2} = 2\sqrt{2}.

12. (c) — inside a shell the field is zero, so the potential does not change with position; it keeps the surface value -GM/R.
